characters: Akorfa: a 12-year-old girl with short braids, a teal JHS uniform and a science notebook.
Obed: her friend, 12, in the same uniform, with round glasses and a habit of asking big questions.
Madam Tawiah: the science teacher, in a green dress and lab coat, who answers questions with questions.
A white-bellied pangolin drawn on the club poster: scaly, with a long tail, curled in a gentle ball.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious young narrator voice; the teacher speaks briefly and asks questions
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and clear, slowing for numbers and units (about 130 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quiet, curious synth with soft forest sounds (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Pangolins live in Ghana’s forests and are shy, ant-eating mammals. The story avoids any claim about how many remain, because numbers change.
The Frozen Zoo is in San Diego, USA; the story uses it as one example of a field called biobanking, which many countries are developing.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm the pangolin species and conservation status for Ghana with the Wildlife Division or IUCN before publication.
Is the description of clones and species recovery accurate and not over-promising?

teacherGuide.overview: A story that leads learners from curiosity to a small experiment to a balanced conclusion: cell banks are insurance, not a replacement for habitat. Run the tomato test so the idea of ice damage is something they have seen.
learningGoals: Explain what a frozen zoo is and why cells, not animals, are kept.
Explain why freezing can damage living cells and how cryoprotectants help.
Evaluate the claim that technology can replace conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies

beforeReading: Ask: what could happen to a species if its forest is cleared?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners to predict what the thawed tomato will look like.
afterReading: Run the tomato test and discuss what the slices show.
Debate: “A frozen zoo means we need not worry about extinction.”
discussion: What does a frozen zoo do well, and what can it not do?
Why did Akorfa say a clone is not a species?
reflection: What place near you could be protected, and who could help?

mathsExtension.task: The Frozen Zoo holds about 11,500 cell lines from about 1,300 species and subspecies. About how many cell lines per species on average?
mathsExtension.answer: 11,500 ÷ 1,300 ≈ 8.8, so about 9 cell lines per species or subspecies.

mathsExtension.task: The Frozen Zoo stores cells at about −196 °C and a home freezer at about −18 °C. How much colder is the Frozen Zoo?

support: Provide a labelled diagram of a cell with ice crystals inside.
stretch: Write a short letter to a wildlife officer explaining one thing a cell bank can and cannot do.

culturalNotes: Pangolins live in Ghana’s forests and are shy, ant-eating mammals. The story avoids any claim about how many remain, because numbers change.
The Frozen Zoo is in San Diego, USA; the story uses it as one example of a field called biobanking, which many countries are developing.
localiseThis: Replace pangolins with another local species your learners know.
Check which species are protected in Ghana and avoid anything that could encourage hunting.

whatWeKnow: Living cells can be frozen at very low temperatures for long periods and later revived.
Clones of a black-footed ferret and a Przewalski’s horse have been produced from cells banked decades earlier.
Protecting habitat is essential for any wild population.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Whether banked cells can rebuild a healthy, genetically varied wild population for many species.
How best to use cell banks together with habitat protection.

investigation.title: What does freezing do to living cells?
steps: An adult cuts two thin slices.
Keep one slice at room temperature on a plate.
Thaw it at room temperature next day.
Compare firmness and look with a hand lens, then draw both slices.
investigation.whatToNotice: The thawed slice is softer and leaks water, because ice damaged many of its cells.
investigation.safetyNote: An adult must cut the tomato. Do not eat the test slices. Wash hands afterwards and throw the slices away.
